name: Abimelech
title: Gideon's son and self-proclaimed ruler over Shechem
summary: Abimelech was the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) and a concubine from Shechem. With ruthless ambition, he obtained silver from the temple of Baal-Berith, hired lawless men, and massacred his seventy half-brothers on one stone in Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, escaped and addressed a sharp prophetic fable to the citizens of Shechem from Mount Gerizim—an allegory about trees that chose a thornbush as their king. Abimelech had himself proclaimed ruler and reigned for three years until God sent an evil spirit to divide him and the leaders of Shechem. Rebellion followed under Gaal, but Abimelech crushed it and laid Shechem in ruins; he scattered salt over the site and set fire to the tower temple of Baal-Berith where about a thousand people had sought refuge. His violent career ended during the siege of Thebez, where a woman shattered his skull with a millstone. To avoid the shame of falling by a woman's hand, he ordered his armor-bearer to run him through. Within the broader context of Judges, this story serves as a warning that power rooted in violence, treachery, and idolatry carries its own judgment—God's righteous retribution strikes those who live by the sword.

keyEvents.title: Abimelech seeks support in Shechem
keyEvents.description: Abimelech persuaded his mother's relatives in Shechem to support him as ruler, and they gave him seventy silver shekels from the temple of Baal-Berith to hire reckless men.

keyEvents.title: The murder of the seventy brothers
keyEvents.description: Abimelech killed his seventy half-brothers, Gideon's sons, on one stone at Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, escaped by hiding.

keyEvents.title: Abimelech proclaimed king
keyEvents.description: The men of Shechem and the citizens of Beth-Millo gathered at the oak in Shechem and proclaimed Abimelech king.

keyEvents.title: Jotham's Fable
keyEvents.description: Jotham called out from Mount Gerizim a fable about the trees choosing a thornbush as king, as a prophetic warning against Abimelech and the men of Shechem. He concluded with a curse upon both parties.

keyEvents.title: The Rebellion in Shechem
keyEvents.description: After three years, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, so that they turned against him. Gaal son of Ebed led a rebellion, but Abimelech fought back with the help of his governor Zebul.

keyEvents.title: The Destruction of Shechem
keyEvents.description: Abimelech captured the city of Shechem, killed its inhabitants, leveled the city to the ground, and sowed salt over it. He also burned the tower temple of Shechem where about a thousand men and women had taken refuge.

keyEvents.title: Abimelech's Death at Thebez
keyEvents.description: During the siege of Thebez, a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull. To avoid the shame of being killed by a woman, he asked his armor-bearer to run him through with his sword. Thus God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done.

versions.summary: Abimelech was a son of the judge Gideon (Jerubbaal) and his concubine from Shechem. He seized power by killing his 70 brothers and had himself proclaimed king over Shechem. His brutal rule ended after three years when he was killed during the siege of Thebez.
versions.title: Gideon's Son and Self-Proclaimed King of Shechem
versions.reason: [minor] Lifespan indicates only an approximate year, not a time span. For someone who lived and died within a short period, it could have been more precise to state, for example, "active c. 1150–1147 BC" or similar. The current wording is acceptable but can be improved.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could mention that Abimelech's story is seen as a warning example of abuse of power and God's righteous judgment, which is theologically central to the narrative.; [minor] Abimelech could also be described as "tyrant" or "usurper" to clarify that his kingship was not legitimate in the biblical sense. The role "self-appointed ruler" could be considered.; [major] Abimelech's mother is not named in the Bible, but she is described as Gideon's concubine (pilegsh) from Shechem (Judg 8:31). Ideally, this field should include a comment or remain blank with a footnote explaining this.; [minor] The list of siblings includes only Jotham. Although the other 69 brothers are not named individually, Jotham is correctly identified as the only named surviving brother. This is acceptable.; [minor] Verses 55–57 in the final event include that the Israelites went home after Abimelech's death and that God repaid Abimelech for his evil. Verses 55–57 are relevant and correctly included.; [minor] The rebellion in the Shechem incident skips some verses (24–25, 27–29, 31–37, 40–44). Although it is not necessary to include all verses, the references could have been more coherent or expanded slightly to better cover the military actions.; [major] Footnotes are missing. This story has rich historical, archaeological, linguistic, and theological background that should be covered.

versions.summary: Abimelech was a son of the judge Gideon (Jerubbaal) and his concubine from Shechem. Driven by ambition, he seized power by killing his 70 brothers on one stone in Ophrah, and had himself proclaimed king over Shechem. Only the youngest brother Jotham escaped and warned the men of Shechem through a well-known fable about trees that chose a thornbush as their king. Abimelech's brutal and illegitimate rule lasted three years before the men of Shechem turned against him. He destroyed Shechem completely, but met his end at Thebez, where a woman dropped a millstone on his head. The story is a powerful biblical witness that abuse of power and bloodshed lead to God's righteous judgment.
versions.title: Gideon's Son and Self-Proclaimed King of Shechem
versions.reason: [major] Gideon had 70 sons (Judg 8:30). Listing only Jotham as a sibling is very incomplete. Even though the 70 brothers were killed, they were still Abimelech's half-brothers. Jotham is the most well-known, but the siblings list should reflect that there were more. At minimum, it should be noted that he had 70 half-brothers, or some of the known names should be included.; [minor] The mother is not named in the Bible, but she is described as Gideon's concubine (pilegsh) from Shechem. It may be useful to set her value to zero while including information about her in the summary, which has already been done.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1150 BC' is reasonable within the traditional chronology of the period of the judges, but there is great uncertainty. Some scholars place this somewhat earlier or later. The phrasing with 'c.' is acceptable.; [minor] The role 'son of Gideon' or 'judge' (some consider him a kind of judge/ruler) could be considered. In Judg 9:22 it says that Abimelech 'ruled over Israel for three years', but he was not a judge in the traditional sense. The current roles are acceptable.; [minor] The footnotes are good and cover relevant aspects. Jotham's fable footnote is marked as 'theological', but it deals more with literary form and political critique – 'linguistic' could have been equally appropriate. However, this is a minor detail.; [minor] The summary is well written and theologically balanced. A small improvement would be to clarify that Abimelech ruled for three years over Israel (not just Shechem), as the text in Judg 9:22 states. The current phrasing may give the impression that he only ruled over Shechem.

versions.summary: Abimelech was the son of the judge Gideon (Jerubbaal) and his concubine from Shechem. Driven by ruthless ambition, he financed his power grab with silver from Baal-Berith's temple, hired lawless men, and killed his seventy half-brothers on one stone in Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, survived and proclaimed from Mount Gerizim a famous fable about trees that chose a thornbush as king—a biting warning against those who supported Abimelech. After having himself declared king, Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years (Judg 9:22). Then God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, so they turned against each other. Abimelech completely destroyed Shechem, scattered salt over its ruins, and burned Baal-Berith's tower temple with a thousand people inside. His brutal conduct ended at the siege of Thebez, where a woman crushed his skull with a millstone. The story of Abimelech is a powerful testimony to God's just retribution: whoever seizes power through violence and deceit will themselves reap the fruit of violence.
versions.title: Gideon's son and self-proclaimed ruler over Shechem
versions.reason: [major] Abimelek had 70 half-brothers (Gideon's sons), not only Jotham. Jotham was the only one who survived the massacre, but the list of siblings should ideally reflect that there were many more brothers and sisters. At minimum, it should be noted that the list is incomplete. The Bible also mentions other of Gideon's sons who are not named individually, but Jotham is the only named survivor.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1150 BC' is reasonable within the period of the judges, though some scholars place Gideon and Abimelek somewhat earlier (c. 1150–1100 BC). It may be more precise to give a range such as 'c. 1150–1120 BC' or similar, to show that this is an approximate lifespan rather than just a single year.; [minor] The description states that Jotham was 'the youngest', but the text in Judges 9:5 says only that he was the youngest (הַקָּטָן). This is correct, yet verse 5 also includes the killing, while verse 6 concerns the men of Shechem proclaiming Abimelek king. The events in verses 5 and 6 are thus two separate actions—the killing and the coronation. It may be worth including a few more verses or splitting them up.; [minor] The footnote on Jotham's fable is classified as 'linguistic', but it deals primarily with literary form and political allegory. 'Other' or 'historical' might have been more fitting, though 'linguistic' can also be defended since it concerns literary genre.; [minor] The summary is good and theologically reflective, but since there are two earlier versions and we must be stricter: the phrasing 'reaps the fruit of violence himself' is good, but the final sentence could with advantage be tied more clearly to the broader theological point in the Book of Judges regarding Israel's cycle of apostasy and its consequences.

footnotes.text: The name Abimelech (אֲבִימֶלֶךְ) means 'my father is king' in Hebrew. This is ironic given that his father Gideon explicitly rejected kingship (Judg 8:23), while Abimelech actively sought it.

The practice of sowing salt over a destroyed city (Judg 9:45) is known from several ancient cultures in the Middle East and symbolized a curse upon the place, expressing the wish that it should never be rebuilt or become fertile again.

Archaeological excavations at Tell Balata, identified as ancient Shechem, have uncovered remains of a large temple that may be linked to the Baal-Berith temple mentioned in Judges 9. Destruction layers from this period have also been found.

Jotham's Fable (Judg 9:7–15) is one of the oldest known fables in world literature. It uses the allegory of trees choosing a worthless thornbush as king as sharp political criticism of Abimelech's illegitimate seizure of power.

Abimelech's death by a millstone thrown by a woman became a well-known motif in Israelite war history. The event is referenced in 2 Sam 11:21, where Joab anticipates that King David will mention it as an example of the dangers of approaching a city wall.

In rabbinic tradition, Abimelech's fate is seen as a clear example of middah keneged middah—that the punishment corresponds to the crime. He who killed his brothers with one stone was himself killed by one stone (the millstone).

Shechem was an important political and religious city in the central highlands. Ba'al-Berit ('Lord of the Covenant') was likely a Canaanite deity, and the temple served as both a religious and political gathering place. The fact that Abimelech financed his power grab with funds from this temple underscores the narrative's point about the destructive consequences of idolatry.

According to Judges 8:30, Gideon had seventy sons, reflecting his many wives and high status. Abimelech was the son of a concubine (pilegsh) from Shechem, which gave him a lower social position among his brothers and may have contributed to his desire to seize power by force.
